answer:
HYPOTHESIS (natural-language answer)

Amber had its highest value in the 4th millennium BCE, peaking in the interval ~3300–3000 BCE, where its z-score reached 1.54 — the dataset maximum. The peak was preceded by a sustained high phase: from ~4000 BCE onward amber's z-score already sat at 1.46 (the second-highest level in the record), making the whole 4th millennium BCE (mean z ≈ 1.49) the amber optimum of the entire 4100 BCE–500 CE series. After the peak, amber collapsed abruptly at the 3rd-millennium transition — falling to z = 0.37/0.02 around 2900–2800 BCE and to negative values (−0.39, then −1.07) through the 3rd millennium and later, never recovering (2nd millennium BCE mean z ≈ −0.56; final centuries of the record ≈ −0.66 to −0.80).

Supporting detail: the amber maximum anchor (BCE 3300, z = 1.54) falls inside the 4th-millennium BCE bin (4000–3001 BCE), so the "highest millennium" and "peak interval" answers are mutually consistent. The interval is reported at the resolution of the underlying 100-year anchors (3300–3000 BCE); the yearly interpolated series is used only to visualize the plateau, not to claim sub-century precision. capital.csv (period groups EN → YBA) cross-checks the same maximum (Zamber = 1.54, group MN = MN the Middle Neolithic, BCE 3300) and extends two 100-year rows earlier (BCE 4300–4200, Zamber = −1.07) without changing the result.

Millennium-bin evidence table (time_series_data.csv; raw anchors at 100-yr steps, interpolated yearly series):

| Millennium | mean z (inter) | max z (inter) | mean z (raw) | max z (raw) | n raw anchors |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1st mil. CE (500 BCE–0) | −0.73 | −0.66 | −0.73 | −0.66 | 6 |
| 2nd mil. BCE | −0.56 | −0.01 | −0.58 | −0.01 | 10 |
| 3rd mil. BCE | −0.28 | 1.54 | −0.15 | 1.54 | 10 |
| **4th mil. BCE** | **+1.49** | **1.54** | **+1.48** | **1.54** | 10 |
| 5th mil. BCE | +0.18* | 1.43* | −1.07 | −1.07 | 1 |

*Edge artifact, disclosed: the 5th-millennium interpolated mean (+0.18) is unreliable — time_series_data.csv starts at CE −4100 with a single raw anchor (BCE 4100, z = −1.07), and the linear interpolation ramps from −1.07 up to +1.46 at BCE 4000, inflating the bin mean. capital.csv's earlier rows (BCE 4300/4200/4100, all z = −1.07) show the true 5th-millennium level was low; this does not affect the 4th-millennium answer.

Note on why the 3rd millennium bin also shows max = 1.54: the 1.54 plateau begins exactly at the BCE 3300 anchor and runs to BCE 3000, so its final year touches the 3rd-millennium bin boundary (bin edge, not a 3rd-millennium peak — bin mean −0.28).

payload.hypothesis: Amber had its highest value in the 4th millennium BCE, peaking in the interval ~3300-3000 BCE (z = 1.54, the dataset maximum), after a sustained high phase at z = 1.46 from ~4000 BCE; after the peak, amber declined sharply at the 3rd-millennium transition and never recovered.
payload.workflow: Loaded time_series_data.csv (3601 yearly rows, CE -4100..-500, BCE as negative CE), capital.csv (39 rows, BCE 4300-500, comma decimals), and the pollen PC1 file (convention check only). Verified Amber_inter is linear interpolation of the 37 raw Amber anchors (100-yr steps) which exactly match capital.csv Zamber. Binned by millennium BCE (4th mil = 4000-3001 BCE): 4th-millennium bin has the highest mean (+1.49) and shares the global max (1.54). Peak plateau = contiguous span where Amber_inter equals the global max (BCE 3300-3000, reported at 100-year anchor resolution); high phase = raw anchors z>=1.46 (BCE 4000-3000). Cross-checked against capital.csv (max Zamber 1.54, group MN, BCE 3300; extra BCE 4300/4200 rows do not change the result). Disclosed the 5th-millennium interpolation edge artifact. Script: analysis_amber_peak.py; outputs: output/amber_peak_results.json.
